caseno: Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 595 of 1963
lawyer:
Shahabuddin Ahmed with A. Halim—For the appellant.
B. N. Chowdhury—For the respondent.
parties:
Meherjan Bibi ------- Appellant
Vs.
Naimuddin Dhali being dead, one of his heirs: Raisuddin Dhali and others ------- Respondents
full_judgment:
5. Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the appellant, contended that the appellate Court below erred in coming to finding that Sada Dhali was the owner at the time of  reparation of CS record without there being any evidence on record to that effect. It erred in law in relying upon the Ext. B and B(I) which have got no relevance at all to the facts and circumstances of the case. Ext. 1 the CS khatian which was prepared some time in 1910 or 1911 shows that Jogesh Chandra Chakraborty was the superior landlord and Adam Munshi alone was in possession of the suit land. Exts. B and B(I) were prepared in 1883 ie. about 30 years before the C. S. operation. In a case between one Uma Sundar Debya and Kamal Prosonna Bal and others. The defendant adduced no evidence to show that Jogesh Chakraborty was in any way connected with either Uma Sundar Debya or Kamal Prosonna Bal, Sada Dhali might have been in possession of some suit plots in 1893 under a different landlord but in the meanwhile with in the course of 30 years the superior landlord of the suit land changed and with the change of the landlord tenants also changed. There is no evidence at all that Sada Dhali continued to be in possession of the entire suit land for the next 30 years. Mr Shahabuddin Ahmed submits that no evidence having been adduced by the defendant as to what happened in the meanwhile the presumption of correctness of entry in the record of rights stand unrebutted. 

 6.. Mr. B. N. Choudhury, the learned advocate for the respondent, has contended that the question whether the presumption as to correctness of entry in the record of rights has been rebutted or not is a question of fact and however erroneously the appellate Court below might have come to that finding of fact, it cannot be interfered with In a second appeal. He had cited several decisions to that effect. 

 "Merely because there Is no evidence to show the basis of the entries in the record of rights, the presumption is not rebutted to view of the provision of section 103(B) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, and also the procedure as laid down in the several sections of the Bengal Tenancy Act followed by the other concerned while preparing the final records of rights. There must be further evidence to show that the entries are incorrect. The absence of evidence for the basis of the entries may be a circumstance which along with other evidence may go to show that the presumption has been rebutted”. 

 8. Yet, the appellate Court below merely because the plaintiff failed to produce any basis of the C.S Khatian held that Sada Dhali was in possession of at least 2 C.S. plots in respect of which the defendant did not file any Chitta papers. This finding cannot be sustained. For it is well settled, as has been held in the case of Aminuddin Biswas Vs, Miajan Biswas, reported in 12 D L R. 103. 'The presumption of correctness, as available on the strength of section 103 B (5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act has got to be rebutted by the person who alleges it.". There was no evidence at all in respect of the said 2 plots that Sada Dhali was in possession even in 1883. In respect of the 10 remaining suit plots the appellate Court below in common with the trial Court held that in some plots Sada Dhali is found to be in exclusive possession and in some other plots he is found to be in Joint possession with Abbas Dhali and others. While the trial Court held that apparently there were great change in possession after the Chitta Dags were prepared, the appellate Court below without any further evidence on record came to hold that Sada Dhali was the owner of the entire suit land. It is no doubt well settled, contended by Mr B.N. Chowdhury that where evidence was led in rebuttal of the presumption of correctness of entry in the record of rights and the appellate Court below comes to a finding that the preemption stands rebutted, that finding is final and cannot be interfered with in the second appellate jurisdiction. In all the decisions cited before me, namely, the case of Wali Mohammad and others Vs. Mohammad Bakhsh, reported in 51 C.L J. 518 Ghulam Mohammad Vs. Secretary of State reported in A.I.R 1938 (L) 445-and Charu Bala Rudra Vs. Narayan Prasad Sen reported in 14 DLR 159 the presumption was rebutted on the basis of relevant evidence on record. In the present case, however, the defendant had not adduced any evidence at all as to what was the state of possession of the suit land at the time of C S. records or approximately earlier to that Mr. B N. Chowdhury submits that by producing Exts. B and B (I) the defendant has discharged the onus of proving that CS khatian has no basis. Thereafter, he argue, it is for the plaintiff to show that her predecessor in interest was in possession of the suit land at the relevant lime. It is difficult to agree with Mr. B.N Chowdhury. By adducing evidence of certain state of affairs 30 years back, how can it be said that the basis of C.S. khatian has been shaken? All that the attendant has produced in this case in the state of affairs relating to 10 out of 82 suit plots as far back as in 1883 which shows superior ownership and possession in the names of a different set of persons. How that evidence is evidence at all in rebuttal of the presumption of correctness of entry in the record of rights is difficult to appreciate. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury has failed to cite a tingle decision to show that evidence of such remote chamber has any bearing upon the presumption of correctness of entry in the record of rights. Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmed has cited the case of Maurabgi Tewari Vs. Kanhaiya Tewari reported In 123 IC 390 in support of his contention that when Chitta Dags and C.S. record show plan of two different persons it must be presumption that at some time between the two periods the person recorded In in the Chitta Dags lost their possession and that the person whose name appears in the C.S. khatian obtained possession, although there Is no presumption regarding the exact time at which the change of affairs took place. I entirely agree with the ratio decidendi of that decision.
